Defective mineralization in growing bone because of various causes
The most common form of rickets in North America is nutritional rickets (ie, vitamin D
deficiency). The most common genetic cause is hypophosphatemia.
Osteogenesis imperfecta
Weak organic bone matrix results in frequent fractures, with severe bowing and deformity in
the more severe types.
Normal intelligence
Gaucher disease
An enzymatic defect leads to overaccumulation of glucocerebrosides (lipids) in many organ
systems, including the bone marrow and the spleen.
Caffey disease
A cortical hyperostosis of infancy (mean age of onset is younger than 9 weeks)
Self-resolving and a diagnosis of exclusion
Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome)
Most common chromosomal abnormality, with incidence of 1 in 800 to 1 in 1,000 live births
and increased incidence with advanced maternal age

Overview
Rickets is a result of defective mineralization in growing bone because of causes,
including nutritional deficiencies and genetic defects. The most common cause of rickets
is vitamin D deficiency, which prevents the body from absorbing the calcium needed for
bone. The most common genetic cause of rickets is genetic hypophosphatemia because
of renal phosphate wasting.
Osteogenesis imperfecta is a result of weakened organic bone matrix from type I
collagen defects. This leads to frequent fractures that may result in severe bowing and
deformities. Osteogenesis imperfecta does not affect intelligence.
Gaucher disease is a metabolic disease caused by an enzyme deficiency that leads to a
buildup of glucocerebrosides in many organs, including the bone marrow. This may
result in bone issues, including fractures.

Caffey disease is a self-limiting disorder characterized by cortical hyperostosis in infancy.
Trisomy 21 is the most common chromosomal abnormality in the United States and the
world; however, the incidence is decreasing with additional prenatal screening. The
incidence increases with advanced maternal age.
Etiology
Rickets
Calcium and phosphate homeostasis is disturbed, leading to poor calcification of the
cartilage matrix of growing long bones.
Radiographic features include widened osteoid seams, metaphyseal cupping, prominence of
the rib heads (osteochondral junction, rachitic rosary), bowing (particularly of the genu
varum), and fractures.
Microscopically, the zone of proliferation is disordered and elongated in the epiphyseal plate.
Genetic causes of rickets include PHEX mutations (X-linked dominant) that lead to an
increased level of fibroblast growth factor-23, causing renal phosphate wasting. This leads to
increased phosphate losses from bone and rickets.
Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome)
Pathoanatomy: typically, two copies of maternal chromosome 21, resulting in three copies of
chromosome 21
Osteogenesis imperfecta
Types I through IV result from a mutation in the COL1A1 and COL1A2 genes, which encode
type I collagen, the mainstay of the organic bone matrix.
The result is bone that has a decreased number of trabeculae and decreased cortical
thickness, referred to as wormian bone.
The specific mutation is identified via DNA analysis of blood.
Other types have no type I collagen mutation but have a similar phenotype and abnormal
bone observed on microscopic examination. Most are a result of collagen processing
mutations.
Gaucher disease
Gaucher disease is the result of a defect in the gene encoding beta-glucocerebrosidase,
which breaks down glucocerebrosides. This leads to macrophages stuffed full of
glucocerebrosides in many organ systems.

Always autosomal recessive
Radiographic findings include Erlenmeyer flask appearance of distal femurs (also observed in
patients with osteopetrosis), osteonecrosis of the hips and femoral condyles, and cortical
thinning.

Etiology
Rickets is a result of a disturbance of calcium and phosphate homeostasis leading to
poor calcification of the cartilage matrix of growing long bones. The classic radiographic
findings include metaphyseal widening; prominence of the rib heads; bowing of the genu
varum; and, in extreme cases, fractures (fractures are rare in young children).
Trisomy 21 typically is the result of an extra copy of maternal chromosome 21 as a result
of nondisjunction at meiosis. Other rarer causes include Robertsonian translocations.
Osteogenesis imperfecta typically results from mutations in one of the two type I
collagen genes (approximately 90% of cases in the United States). One other dominant
type exists (type V osteogenesis imperfecta). The other cases are recessive, all severe,
and typically present at birth. They mostly result from mutations in collagen-processing
genes. The phenotypes are similar, and management is identical.
Gaucher disease is an autosomal recessive disease caused by mutations in the GBA
gene. It may very in severity, with the most severe cases affecting the central nervous
system and other organs.

Osteogenesis imperfecta
Osteogenesis imperfecta currently is classified into 19 different types based on genetic
mutation.
The most common types are type I through type IV, which are the result of mutations in one
of the type I collagen genes, COL1A1 or COL1A2. These mutations are inherited dominantly
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:31 PM
AAOS | Other Conditions With Musculoskeletal Involvement
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003012
6/14

and range from a very severe, often lethal phenotype (type II) to a milder phenotype with few
fractures in childhood but early-onset adult osteoporosis (type I). Type III typically manifests
as deforming fractures in childhood that require surgical rodding, and type IV manifests as
multiple childhood fractures with or without deformities.
Other types of osteogenesis imperfecta may result from dominant or recessive mutations
and typically have a more severe childhood manifestation.
Evaluation and Diagnosis
Patient History
Rickets
A history of being breast-fed and having little sun exposure is the most likely scenario for
vitamin D–deficiency rickets.
Older patients with unusual diets also should be evaluated.

Patient History
For patients with nutritional rickets, the physician should consider a careful dietary
history. Because breast milk is low in vitamin D, if patients do not receive
supplementation, they will become vitamin D deficient. Older patients with restricted
diets, especially if they live in the northern United States where sun exposure is limited,
also are at risk for rickets.
Physical Examination
Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome)
Phenotypic features include a flattened face; upward slanting eyes with epicanthal folds; a
single palmar crease; intellectual disability (varies); congenital heart disease (endocardial
cushion defect in 50% of patients); duodenal atresia; hypothyroidism; hearing loss;
ligamentous laxity; and a high incidence of leukemia and lymphoma, diabetes mellitus, and
Alzheimer disease later in adult life.
Spine

7/14

Atlantoaxial instability is present in 9% to 22% of patients; it is controversial whether flexion
and extension cervical spine views are necessary before sports participation.
Scoliosis is present in as many as 50% of patients.
Spondylolisthesis is present in as many as 6% of patients.
Metatarsus primus varus, pes planovalgus, and hallux valgus in the feet are common.
Patellar dislocation, pain, and instability are common.
Hip instability (often late) is common, occasionally with only mild bony abnormality.
Osteogenesis imperfecta
Osteogenesis imperfecta should be considered in children undergoing a nonaccidental
trauma workup. In addition, osteogenesis imperfecta also should be considered all children
who have three or more fractures before the teenage years or any spinal compression
fractures without a known medical cause.
Particularly in types II and III, basilar invagination and severe scoliosis may occur.
Olecranon apophyseal avulsion fractures are characteristic; children presenting with these
fractures should be evaluated for osteogenesis imperfecta.
Associated dentinogenesis imperfecta, hearing loss, blue sclera, joint hyperlaxity, and
wormian skull bones (puzzle piece appearance to the skull after fontanel closure) are
observed.
Gaucher disease
Three forms are identified based on age of onset.
Type 1 (adult): easy bruising (thrombocytopenia), anemia, enlarged liver and/or spleen,
bone pain and/or fractures
Type 2 (infantile): enlarged spleen and/or liver by age 3 months; brain involved, lethal by
age 2 years.
Type 3 (juvenile): onset in teenage years, thrombocytopenia, anemia, enlarged liver and/or
spleen, bone pain and/or fractures, gradual and mild brain involvement
Caffey disease
Bones of the jaw (mandible) and forearm (ulna) are most affected, with diffuse cortical
thickening; however, any bone except the vertebrae and phalanges may be affected.
Febrile illness with hyperirritability, swelling of soft tissues, and cortical thickening of the
bone are present.
The result of COL1A1 mutations (same as osteogenesis imperfecta)


Physical Examination
The characteristic facial features of trisomy 21 include a flattened face with upward
slanting eyes, epicanthal folds, and a single palmar crease. Intellectual disability occurs
to varying degrees. Congenital cardiac disease, duodenal atresia, and thyroid disease
also are common. Patients may have ligamentous laxity, especially in childhood, and
hearing loss, especially as they age.
In general, osteogenesis imperfecta should be considered in the following situations:
nonaccidental trauma evaluations, patients with three or more fractures before the
teenage years, any spinal compression fractures in childhood, and patients with low
bone density without a medical explanation. Genetic panels that include all the known
genes for osteogenesis imperfecta are readily available at clinical testing laboratories. In
patients with severe osteogenesis imperfecta, basilar invagination and severe scoliosis
may occur and require management. Olecranon avulsion fractures are common; if a
child presents with an olecranon avulsion fracture, the physician should evaluate the
child for osteogenesis imperfecta. Other associated features include dentinogenesis
imperfecta, hearing loss (may not occur until adulthood), blue sclera, joint hyperlaxity
(more common in childhood), and wormian skull bones.
Gaucher disease manifests with different levels of severity. Type 1 is the most common,
and these patients typically do not have symptoms until adulthood. They have bone pain
and fractures. Patients with type 2 present in infancy and usually die by age 2 years
without treatment because of neurologic decline. Patients with type 3 have childhood
onset with mild brain involvement.
Patients with Caffey disease present in infancy with diffuse cortical thickening, typically
of the jaw and forearm; however, any bone may be involved (except the vertebrae and
phalanges). Patients often have fevers and soft-tissue swelling. The disease usually
resolves by 9 months of age. Although Caffey disease is the result of COL1A1 mutations,
patients do not go on to develop osteogenesis imperfecta.

Laboratory Studies
Rickets
Serum calcium, phosphorus, alkaline phosphatase, parathyroid hormone (PTH), and 25-
hydroxyvitamin D levels must be evaluated to assess the cause.
Gaucher disease
A white blood cell count for enzyme activity is diagnostic.
Caffey disease
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and alkaline phosphatase level are elevated; however,
cultures are negative.
Pathologic examination results show hyperplasia of collagen fibers and fibrinoid
degeneration.

Laboratory Studies
If rickets is being considered in a patient, surgeons must assess serum calcium,
phosphorus, alkaline phosphatase, PTH, and 25-hydroxyviatmin D levels to differentiate
between nutritional rickets and hypophosphatemic rickets. Surgeons also should
consider referral to endocrinology.
Similar to mucopolysaccharidoses, Gaucher disease is an enzyme defect; therefore, it
can be diagnosed via an enzyme assay. Genetic testing also is available.
Caffey disease generally is a diagnosis of exclusion. Markers of inflammation, such as
erythrocyte sedimentation rate, are elevated, with negative cultures. Alkaline
phosphatase level is elevated with no signs of rickets. COL1A1 test results are positive,
and the patients will not go on to develop osteogenesis imperfecta.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Techniques and Procedures

10/14

Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome)
Supportive brace management is indicated for feet and knees and for reducible hips in
patients younger than 6 years.
Management of an asymptomatic atlantodental interval of 5 to 10 mm is controversial;
observation via MRI to assess the spinal cord is common.
Osteogenesis imperfecta
Manage fractures with the use of light splints.
Diphosphonates are used; diphosphonates inhibit osteoclasts, yielding increased cortical
thickness with decreased fracture rates and pain.
Gaucher disease
Enzyme replacement therapy currently is available and helps manage all symptoms except
neurologic symptoms.
Caffey disease
Management is supportive, with occasional glucocorticoid use; no indications for surgical
management.
Surgical Management
Techniques and Procedures
Surgical Approaches
Rickets
Surgical management is indicated for lower extremity bowing that does not resolve after
medical management of rickets.
Hemiepiphysiodesis or osteotomy may be indicated.
Comanagement with an endocrinologist is recommended because many medical therapeutic
options are available.
Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome)
Fusion is always indicated if spinal cord compromise is observed on MRIs or if an
atlantodental interval greater than 5 is observed in a patient with symptoms; however, fusion
is associated with a high (as high as 50%) complication rate.
Soft-tissue surgery fails because of ligamentous laxity and hypotonia; therefore, if surgical
management is performed, bony realignment is indicated (ie, pelvic osteotomy for hip
instability, tibial tubercle osteotomy for lateral patellar dislocation).
Osteogenesis imperfecta

For severe bowing of the extremities or recurrent fracture, intramedullary fixation is
indicated with or without osteotomy. Telescoping rods allow for growth (Figure 1).
Progressive scoliosis and basilar invagination are managed via spinal fusion.
Gaucher disease
Enzyme replacement therapy is available.

hip-to-ankle radiograph demonstrates a femoral deformity. B, Postoperative frog-lateral
fluoroscopic image of the hip and femur shows osteotomies and fixation with the use of a
telescoping rod. (Reproduced from Spencer SA: Pediatric musculoskeletal disorders and
syndromes, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL,
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 1351-1360.)

Surgical Management
Rickets is managed surgically if lower extremity bowing does not respond to medical
management. This may require hemiepiphysiodesis or osteotomy. An endocrinologist

via fibroblast growth factor-23 antibody therapy for hypophosphatemic rickets to stop
phosphate wasting.
